questions.section: The question a carpet plot answers
questions.question: The constraint diagram gives the feasible WTO/S and TSL/WTO. What does a carpet plot add to it?
options: The takeoff weight WTO over a grid of the two, from runs of the sizing code
The minimum TSL/WTO at each WTO/S, from the constraint equations
A design point found by matching the constraint lines, with no run of the sizing code
The aspect ratio that gives the lowest WTO at the chosen design point
questions.explanation: The constraint diagram does not show WTO. The carpet plot draws WTO from converged sizing runs over the grid, with the constraint lines on it, so the lightest feasible point can be read.

questions.question: In the fighter example of the lecture, the takeoff distance on the TSL/WTO = 0.9 curve runs from 670 ft at 50 lb/ft² to 1,070 ft at 70 lb/ft², against a limit of 500 ft. What does the cross-plot give for that curve?
options: No takeoff crossing: the curve fails the takeoff limit at every wing loading of the matrix
A takeoff crossing below 50 lb/ft², read by extending the quadratic past the runs
No takeoff crossing: the curve passes the takeoff limit at every wing loading of the matrix
No takeoff crossing, so the takeoff constraint is not active anywhere on the plot
questions.explanation: Takeoff fails above 500 ft, and all three runs of the 0.9 curve lie above it, so the curve fails everywhere inside the matrix. Crossings are read inside the matrix only, and the takeoff line still crosses the 1.0 and 1.1 curves.

questions.section: Step 5: read the lightest feasible point
questions.question: In the fighter example of the lecture, the runs of 56,000 lb and 49,000 lb meet every limit, and the lowest shaded point on the sizing plot is 46,300 lb at 56 lb/ft² and TSL/WTO = 1.017. What comes next?
options: Rerun the sizing code at 56 lb/ft² and 1.017 and check the rerun against every limit
Report the 49,000 lb run, the lightest of the nine that meets every limit
Report 46,300 lb as read, since every shaded point already meets every limit
Report the 43,700 lb center run, the design point chosen from the constraint diagram
questions.explanation: The plot interpolates between runs, so only the rerun at the point read from it is a converged design, and it must meet every limit. It is 2,700 lb lighter than the best run; the center run misses the takeoff limit, 595 ft against 500 ft.

questions.question: In the fighter example of the lecture, the offset uses (TSL/WTO)1 = 0.9 and k = 60 lb/ft². At what abscissa ξ is the run at WTO/S = 60 lb/ft² and TSL/WTO = 1.1 drawn on the carpet plot?
options: ξ = 72 lb/ft²
ξ = 60 lb/ft²
ξ = 66 lb/ft²
ξ = 126 lb/ft²
questions.explanation: ξ = 60 + 60 (1.1 − 0.9) = 72 lb/ft²: the 1.1 curve moves 12 lb/ft² to the right. The abscissa is not the wing loading, which is read from the lines of the grid.

questions.question: The fighter study adds the aspect ratio as a third design variable and runs AR = 4, 5, and 6. How is the aspect ratio chosen?
options: Fit the lightest feasible WTO of each AR, read the minimum, and run a new matrix at that AR
Vary AR at the lightest feasible point of the AR = 5 matrix, with WTO/S and TSL/WTO held
Take whichever of 4, 5, and 6 gives the lowest lightest feasible WTO
Fit the lightest feasible WTO of each AR and report the minimum of the fit as the answer
questions.explanation: Each AR moves the feasible region and its lowest point, so each needs its own matrix and lightest feasible point. The quadratic finds the minimum between the values run, and a matrix, a carpet plot, and a rerun at that AR confirm it.

questions.question: The lightest feasible point of the fighter example lies on the takeoff line, with Ps = 217 ft/s and an acceleration time of 47.3 s against 50 s. How is the point reported?
options: Takeoff as the active constraint, and Ps and acceleration with their margins
All three constraints as active, since the point meets all three limits
Acceleration as the active constraint, since its 2.7 s margin is the smallest
Takeoff as the active constraint, with nothing on the other two since they are met
questions.explanation: An active constraint closes the feasible region at the point, and here only the takeoff line does. The others are reported with their margins: 217 ft/s against 0 ft/s, and 47.3 s against 50 s.

questions.section: Sensitivities at the lightest feasible point
questions.question: At the lightest feasible point of the fighter example, WTO = 46,300 lb, TSL/WTO = 1.017, and ∂WTO/∂(TSL/WTO) ≈ 56,300 lb per unit. What is the sensitivity sx to TSL/WTO?
questions.explanation: sx = (1.017/46,300) × 56,300 = 1.24, so 1% more TSL/WTO gives about 1.24% more WTO. Dividing the derivative by WTO alone, without the factor x, gives 1.22.

questions.section: Sensitivities at the lightest feasible point
questions.question: In the fighter example, WTO stays within 200 lb along the takeoff line from 53 to 60 lb/ft². Why is the minimum along the line this flat?
options: Along the line both variables rise, and their opposite effects on WTO cancel at the point
Both sensitivities are near zero at the lightest feasible point, as at any minimum
The takeoff constraint holds WTO fixed at every point of its line
The 2% step of the central difference is too coarse to show the change
questions.explanation: Up the takeoff line WTO/S and TSL/WTO both rise. With sx = −0.58 for WTO/S and 1.24 for TSL/WTO, the two changes cancel at the point; neither sensitivity is small.
